item.title: Sri Lanka central bank has no credit target, backs borrowing within repayment capacity: Governor
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Weerasinghe noted that sustaining credit expansion above 20 percent for two consecutive years is rare in Sri Lanka
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s Central Bank does not set a specific target for credit growth and is encouraging people and businesses to borrow if they have the ability to repay, Governor Nandalal Weerasinghe told reporters.

Weerasinghe rejected suggestions that the public should delay taking loans, noting that borrowing at current market interest rates supports economic activity when backed by genuine needs, business opportunities, and repayment capacity across sectors.

“At this moment, according to the prevailing interest rates, if one has the ability to borrow, one should definitely take a loan,” Weerasinghe said.

Total credit in the economy is currently growing by more than 20 percent, easing only slightly from around 24 to 25 percent recorded during the 2024–25 post-crisis recovery period.

Weerasinghe noted that sustaining credit expansion above 20 percent for two consecutive years is rare in Sri Lanka’s history and shows that loan supply remains strong.

“Credit growth being over 20 percent means we currently see it as a very good provision of credit to the economy,” the Governor said.

Addressing questions on a recent Central Bank Credit Supply Survey, which pointed to rising loan demand alongside tighter supply, Weerasinghe denied that banks are discouraging lending.

He explained that low interest rates have naturally boosted borrowing demand, while banks must still check each borrower’s repayment ability, project feasibility, and risk under central bank rules before granting loans.

Rather than targeting a fixed lending figure, the Central Bank watches how total borrowing by both the private sector and the government affects overall domestic demand—known as aggregate demand — especially for imports, and whether that demand pushes up inflation.

He added that taking a loan remains each person’s individual decision based on repayment strength, while the Central Bank uses market interest rates simply to adjust overall demand up or down. (Colombo/Nov20/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka market rates rose after May hike: Central bank
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: ECONOMYNEXT – Market interest rates in Sri Lanka have risen steadily since May 2026, the Central Bank said as it raised its policy rate by another 25 basis points to 9 percent to curb rising inflation. Following a 100-basis-point rate hike in May 2026, borrowing and lending rates across the financial system adjusted upward, Lasitha […]
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Market interest rates in Sri Lanka have risen steadily since May 2026, the Central Bank said as it raised its policy rate by another 25 basis points to 9 percent to curb rising inflation.

Following a 100-basis-point rate hike in May 2026, borrowing and lending rates across the financial system adjusted upward, Lasitha Pathberiya, Director of the Economic Research Department at the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, said.

“Since the monetary policy tightening in May 2026 by 100 basis points, we see the adjustment in market interest rates in line with this monetary policy tightening in May,” Pathberiya said.

The interbank call money rate rose by 108 basis points, the one-year Treasury bill rate increased by 146 basis points, and the weekly prime lending rate climbed by 166 basis points since the May tightening.

The rupee has held steady, he claimed, despite global uncertainty from the conflict in West Asia, while central bank dollar purchases lifted gross official reserves to 7.1 billion dollars amid debt service payments.

“The Sri Lankan Rupee remained broadly stable in recent weeks. In the month of November so far, the rupee depreciated by 0.06%, while overall the rupee depreciated by 6.9% so far in 2026,” he said.

The central bank bought around 1.7 billion dollars from the market up to October, with substantial purchases continuing in November.

Because these dollar purchases added excess cash to the banking system, pushing market liquidity to around 450 billion rupees, the Monetary Policy Board also raised the Statutory Reserve Requirement by 1 percentage point to 3 percent from December 9 to absorb 150 billion rupees permanently.

Private sector credit growth has slowed slightly but remains high at 21.8 percent, while headline inflation reached 8.3 percent in October due to higher energy and food costs. (Colombo/Nov20/2026)

item.title: LankaPay reports security incident at LankaSign registration portal
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: The breach potentially exposed personal information including names, National Identity Card (NIC) numbers, email address
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s national payment network operator, LankaPay (Pvt) Ltd, said a data collection portal used to register for its LankaSign service recently experienced a ‘security incident’ that may have compromised users’ personal details.

In a notice signed by Deputy Chief Executive Officer Dinuka Perera, the firm stated that the breach potentially exposed personal information including names, National Identity Card (NIC) numbers, email addresses, and mobile numbers.

LankaPay said the incident was strictly confined to the registration data collection portal and did not affect any core infrastructure.

“This incident is confined only to the above data collection portal, and no other systems including payment systems or digital signature platforms have been affected or impacted,” the notice stated.

The company said it has taken appropriate steps to contain the breach and is monitoring the situation.

Affected users or those seeking further clarification have been advised to contact LankaPay’s Data Protection Officer, Lakmal Uyanahewage, via email at dpo@lankapay.net.

Regulated by the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, LankaPay operates the country’s national payment network and serves as a certification authority issuing digital signatures through its LankaSign platform. (Colombo/Nov20/2026)

item.title: Fitch assigns Asia Asset Finance’s Rs3bn debt ‘A-(lka)’ rating
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: The proposed debentures will have a maturity of five years and will be listed on the Colombo Stock Exchange.
item.content:encoded:
Fitch Ratings – Singapore: Fitch Ratings has assigned Asia Asset Finance PLC’s (AAF, A+(lka)/Stable) proposed Sri Lankan rupee-denominated subordinated listed debentures of up to LKR3 billion a final National Long-Term Rating of ‘A-(lka)’.

The proposed debentures will have a maturity of five years and will be listed on the Colombo Stock Exchange. The company plans to use the proceeds to strengthen its Tier 2 capital base and support loan-book expansion.

The final rating is the same as the expected rating assigned on 26 October 2026 and follows the receipt of documents conforming to information already received.

Key Rating Drivers

The proposed subordinated debentures are rated two notches below AAF’s National Long-Term Rating. This reflects our baseline notching for loss severity for this debt class and our expectation of poor recoveries in the event of default.

We applied our Bank Rating Criteria to rate the proposed debentures, as we view the prudential capital framework of Sri Lankan finance companies as closer to that of banks. There is no additional notching for non-performance risk, as the proposed debentures do not contain going-concern loss-absorption features.

AAF’s National Long-Term Rating of ‘A+(lka)’ with Stable Outlook reflects our expectation that India-based Muthoot Finance Ltd (MFL, BB+/Stable) would provide extraordinary support to its Sri Lankan subsidiary, if required. This view takes into account MFL’s ability to support AAF, underpinned by the parent’s standalone profile as India’s largest gold-backed lender. We also consider MFL’s 78.4% shareholding in AAF, record of ordinary equity support and its strategic and operational alignment with AAF in gold-backed lending.

Even so, AAF’s strategic importance to MFL is constrained by its small size, modest group role, low contribution, limited brand sharing and operations in a different jurisdiction. AAF’s standalone credit profile does not drive its rating, but we assess it as significantly weaker than its support-driven rating.

See our commentary, Fitch Affirms Asia Asset Finance at ‘A+(lka)’; Outlook Stable for details on AAF’s key rating drivers and sensitivities.

RATING SENSITIVITIES

Factors that Could, Individually or Collectively, Lead to Negative Rating Action/Downgrade
A downgrade of AAF’s National Long-Term Rating would lead to a downgrade of the subordinated debt rating.

Factors that Could, Individually or Collectively, Lead to Positive Rating Action/Upgrade
An upgrade of AAF’s National Long-Term Rating would lead to an upgrade of the subordinated debt rating.

item.title: Sri Lanka inflation projected to reach 9-pct by month-end: Central Bank Governor
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: "Inflation is going to remain elevated in the near term, at higher than expected levels compared to the last review," Na
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s headline inflation is projected to remain elevated in the near term, reaching around 9 percent, higher than the central bank’s earlier expectations, CBSL Governor Nandalal Weerasinghe said explaining the rationale behind the monetary policy rate hike.

CBSL raised its key monetary policy rate by 25 basis points on Friday (20) and increased commercial banks’ Statutory Reserve Ratio (SRR) by 1 percent in a surprise move citing higher inflation and credit growth.

“Inflation is going to remain elevated in the near term, at higher than expected levels compared to the last review,” Nandalal told reporters.

“If you look at this chart, it shows the middle path of the fan chart, which appears that inflation, headline inflation, is likely to reach 9% by end of this month, and it will remain around that level, well, a little bit higher or lower around that level in the near term.”

“This was higher than what we expected, especially when we took the monetary — earlier decision to tighten back in May.

Sri Lanka’s overall rate of inflation, as measured by the Colombo Consumer Price Index (CCPI), rose to more than three-year high of 8.3 percent in October 2026, up from the previous month’s 8.0 percent and breached the Central Bank’s upper inflation target rate of 7 percent for the fourth month.

“If you look at the inflation expectations surveys, yes, the short-term inflation expectations, they are still a bit… the curve has shifted a little upwards, it seems.

“Headline inflation is running relatively higher than what is expected, so based on that, the major decision we have to take today is to bring the inflation back to our targeted range as soon as possible.”

The CBSL expects inflation to begin stabilizing and returning to target levels by the second half of next year.

As a second measure, CBSL also raised the Statutory Reserve Ratio (SRR) by 1 percent.

“That’s, we think, the appropriate decision at this point because SRR is not a traditional, conventional instrument to use for monetary policy purposes.

“Given the situation that there has been a significant amount of excess structural liquidity in the market, I think about 460 billion structural, that we have been conducting auctions on a regular basis, so I think it’s a good opportunity for us to absorb liquidity on a permanent basis.

“This is a good opportunity for us to use this instrument to absorb on a permanent basis. I think 1% will bring in about 150 — close to 150 billion liquidity will come into the — come back into the Central Bank.”

The overall liquidity situation has enough space up to 460 billion, Weerasinghe said.

“Even if you take 150 billion, we have flexibility to inject or manage liquidity for us to be able to maintain short-term interest rates where we think appropriate, in line with our monetary policy stance.

“So that’s the liquidity management—we have some flexibility for us to maintain inflation and short-term interest rates — and also to absorb some of the excess liquidity.

“That is to prevent higher expansion of credit in the economy by the banking sector, that will control that. As a result, we think we can bring the inflation back to target level sooner.” (Colombo/Nov20/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka lawmakers weigh asset sales, legal action over Sanasa crisis
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: A financial crisis at the Gampaha District Sanasa Society has made it unable to repay depositors
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – A Sri Lankan parliamentary subcommittee is looking at selling assets and taking legal action to recover funds and repay depositors affected by a financial crisis at the Gampaha District Sanasa Society, according to a parliament statement.

The subcommittee, appointed by the Committee on Public Accounts (COPA) to investigate crises in the cooperative sector, met on November 16 under the chairmanship of parliamentarian Ruwanthilaka Jayakody.

Lawmakers examined an Auditor General’s report highlighting management weaknesses at the society, where funds were allegedly invested in private companies without required approvals.

Those unauthorized investments left the society unable to repay deposits held by both its members and external customers, the statement said.

To address the fallout, the COPA subcommittee has prioritized liquidating society assets, including lifting existing court injunctions, and distributing available funds to depositors fairly.

Lawmakers are also pursuing surcharges against former board members, taking legal action against the private firm involved, and resuming unfinished projects to generate revenue.

The panel also evaluated regulatory shortcomings within the Department of Cooperatives alongside provincial and district officials. (Colombo/Nov20/2026)

Key Rating Drivers

The proposed senior unsecured debentures are rated at the same level as AAF’s National Long-Term Rating in accordance with Fitch’s criteria. This is because the issue will rank equally with the claims of the company’s other senior unsecured creditors.

AAF’s National Long-Term Rating reflects our expectation that its India-based parent, Muthoot Finance Ltd (MFL, BB+/Stable), would provide extraordinary support, if required. This takes into account MFL’s ability to support its Sri Lanka-based subsidiary, underpinned by MFL’s standalone profile and position as India’s largest gold-backed lender. We also consider MFL’s majority 78.4% shareholding in AAF, record of ordinary equity support and strategic and operational alignment with AAF in gold-backed lending.

Even so, AAF’s strategic importance to MFL is constrained by its small size, modest group role, low contribution, limited brand sharing and operations in a different jurisdiction. AAF’s standalone credit profile does not drive its rating, but we assess it as significantly weaker than its support-driven rating.

See, Fitch Affirms Asia Asset Finance at ‘A+(lka)’; Outlook Stable, for details on AAF’s key rating drivers and sensitivities.

item.title: Sri Lanka regulator extends Sanasa Life Insurance suspension
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: The suspension will be in effect for the three weeks from November 19 to December 10.
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – The Insurance Regulatory Commission of Sri Lanka has extended the suspension of the registration granted to Sanasa Life Insurance Co PLC to carry on long-term insurance businesses, the company said in a market filing.

The suspension will be in effect for the three weeks from November 19 to December 10.

The registration was suspended in terms of Section 18(2) of the regulation of Insurance Industry Act, No:43 of 2000 (RII Act).

Sri Lanka regulator suspends Sanasa Life Insurance

The registration was suspended last December for:
– Conducting business in a manner which could be detrimental to the interest of the policy holders/insurance industry and national interest.
– Not being able to meet the solvency margin specified by the regulator.
– Has failed to follow the provisions of the Regulation of Insurance Industry Act and the order s/rules and conditions made by the regulator under the said Act.
– Providing data which are false/inaccurate and misleading and has failed/concealed the material facts.
(Colombo/Nov20/2026)

item.title: Open-source firm WSO2 rebrands as Choreo Labs to focus on AI agent control
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Choreo comes from choreography — keeping agents, systems, and identities moving in step — while Labs reflects engineerin
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Open-source software company WSO2 has changed its name to Choreo Labs as businesses put artificial intelligence (AI) agents into daily operations and need stronger control over what those tools access.

Founded in 2005 during the web services era, the company builds software that connects enterprise systems and manages digital identities.

“Enterprises won’t put agents into production until they can see, govern, and trust every action those agents take,” Choreo Labs CEO Harry Ault said.

The company said “Choreo” comes from choreography — keeping agents, systems, and identities moving in step — while “Labs” reflects its engineering culture.

As AI agents act on their own — with non-human traffic overtaking human traffic online in May 2026, according to Cloudflare — businesses must track every system, data record, and identity an agent uses.

Choreo Labs brings its API, integration, identity, and agent tools onto one platform called Choreo, including its open-source Choreo Agent Manager, which gives each agent a verified identity, applies over 40 built-in safety rules, and can stop any agent with one click.

“Before an agent goes live, those clients want to know who it is, what it’s allowed to touch, and what it did,” Tech Mahindra’s Chockalingam Subramanian said.

Existing customers do not need to take any action, as current products, contracts, support, and open-source licences remain unchanged.

Other product names will move to the new brand over the coming months.

Choreo Labs will make its first appearance under its new name at AWS re:Invent in Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, 2026. (Colombo/Nov20/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka Central Bank raises key policy rate, SRR citing high inflation, credit growth
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: In May, the OPR was raised by 100 bps
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s Central Bank raised its key monetary policy rate by 25 basis points on Friday (20) and increased commercial banks’ Statutory Reserve Ratio (SRR) by 1 percent in a surprise move citing higher inflation and credit growth.

The Monetary Policy Board, at its meeting held Thursday (19), decided to increase the Overnight Policy Rate (OPR) by 25 basis points (bps) to 9.00%.

It also raised SRR by 1 percentage point to 3.00% with effect from December 9, 2026.

“Market interest rates have materially adjusted in response to the monetary policy tightening measures effected in May 2026. Growth of credit to the private sector has continued to slow, although it still remains high,” the Central Bank said in its monetary policy statement.

Markets had been betting on an unchanged monetary policy stance.

The latest move comes amid gradual depreciation in the rupee currency and foreign outflows from the government securities.

“The ongoing conflict in the Middle East has lasted longer than expected. Elevated global energy prices together with rising food prices have continued to fuel inflationary pressures domestically, causing inflation to increase to 8.3% (y-o-y) in October 2026. Core inflation also rose, reflecting spillovers from higher energy and food prices.”

“Global energy prices have eased somewhat recently. However, the second-round effects of previous increases in energy prices are expected to exert price pressures in the near term.”

“Latest projections also showed that inflation could remain higher in the near term and for longer than previously projected, before returning to the target of 5% in the second half of 2027. Inflation expectations, particularly in the one-year period ahead, have also risen recently, although medium-term inflation expectations remain anchored around the target.”

The external sector remained resilient despite uncertainty in the global economy, it said.

“Amid the Government’s debt service payments, continued net foreign exchange purchases by the Central Bank helped increase Sri Lanka’s gross official reserves to around USD 7.1 bn  by end October 2026, while the Sri Lanka rupee remained broadly stable.”

“In view of the elevated inflation outlook in the near term, the Board was of the view that a further tightening of the monetary policy stance would be required to minimise the risk of de-anchoring inflation expectations. Such tightening of policy reflects the Board’s continued commitment to maintaining domestic price stability.”

“Moreover, the buildup of officials reserves through foreign exchange purchases by the Central Bank from the domestic market has resulted in a substantial increase in rupee liquidity in the domestic money market. This could slow the envisaged moderation of credit expansion in the period ahead. Accordingly, the Board also decided to increase the Statutory Reserve Requirement (SRR) by 1 percentage point to 3.00% with effect from the reserve maintenance period commencing 09 December 2026.”

£The Central Bank will carefully assess incoming data on the domestic and global fronts and emerging risks, and stand ready to take measures, as appropriate, to ensure that inflation stabilises around the target, while supporting the economy to reach its potential over the medium term.”

Central Bank Governor Nandalal Weerasinghe early this month told an investor forum that rise in inflation was mainly due to high energy prices and the Central Bank was considering if the monetary policy should be tightened for a cost-push inflation from the supply side. (Colombo/November 20/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka’s IRD surpasses 2026 revenue target after Customs
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: The government has revised up the 2026 total tax revenue target to Rs.5,478bn from Rs.4,910bn
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s main tax collector, the Inland Revenue Department (IRD), surpassed its 2026 revenue target of Rs. 2,402 billion this week, the government said, a month after the island nation’s Customs breached its goal for this year.

The IRD surpassed the target on Monday (16) after successfully collecting Rs. 2,441.9 billion.

The Finance Ministry quoting the IRD said the revenue collection has increased by Rs. 491 billion compared to November 16, 2025, representing a growth of 115 percent.

“The growth reflects strengthened tax administration, greater efficiency in tax revenue collection, and a growing inclination among the public to comply with tax laws and regulations,” the Finance Ministry said.

Sri Lanka Customs has already surpassed its 2026 revenue target of Rs. 2,207 billion on October 13, and it has collected Rs. 2,469 billion as of Tuesday (17).

“Revenue collected in excess of targets by government revenue-collecting agencies provides financial strength to reduce the government’s debt burden and lower debt interest payments,” the Finance Ministry said.

Sri Lanka has already revised up its 2026 tax revenue by 11.6 percent to Rs. 5,478 billion. Originally, the government had estimated Rs. 4,910 billion revenues from taxes for this year.

The island nation’s tax revenue is expected to increase 15.5 percent of the gross domestic products (GDP) this year, more than double from what it was in 2022 when Sri Lanka declared bankruptcy. (Colombo/November 19/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka MP defends stalled Rs100mn pet cemetery promised in last budget
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: Promised in previous budget to house stray dogs from Colombo and its suburbs and provide cemetery and cremation services
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka parliamentarian Lakshman Nipuna Arachchi defended progress on a 100 million rupee budget-allocated dog shelter in the Piliyandala-Kesbewa area, stating that land release and legal procurement procedures caused delays but insisting the funds were not wasted.

The exchange took place in parliament after an opposition lawmaker questioned whether the government had built the facility promised in the previous budget to house stray dogs from Colombo and its suburbs and provide cemetery and cremation services.

“I am asking Lakshman Nipuna Arachchi by name whether you all at least built that pet facility,” Samagi Jana Balawegaya MP Nallin Bandara questioned, noting that 100 million had been allocated for the project in last year’s Budget.

Sri Lanka budget 2026: cemetery and cremation facilities for pets

Responding in parliament, Nipuna Arachchi acknowledged implementation hurdles but maintained that work had not halted.

Nipuna Arachchi said the selected site belonged to the Public Trustee and required formal release before the government could proceed with strict legal procurement processes.

“We got those released in the proper manner, and after that, we carried out the necessary procurement work. It hasn’t stopped,” Nipuna Arachchi claimed, adding that preliminary structural work is currently underway at the site.

“That means the money has not been completely wasted,” he said. (Colombo/Nov19/2026)

item.title: Fitch upgrades 6, affirms 2 Sri Lankan insurers’ IFS ratings on scale recalibration
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: The insurers' National Ratings take into consideration their creditworthiness relative to those of other issuers in the
item.content:encoded:
Fitch Ratings – Colombo – 19 Nov 2026: Fitch Ratings has taken the following actions on the National Insurer Financial Strength (IFS) Ratings on eight Sri Lankan insurers following recalibration of the agency’s Sri Lankan national rating scale following the recent sovereign rating upgrade:

— Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation Life Limited (SLIC Life): National IFS Rating upgraded to ‘AA-(lka) from ‘A+(lka)’; Outlook Stable

— Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation General Limited (SLIC General): National IFS Rating upgraded to ‘AA-(lka) from ‘A+(lka)’; Outlook Stable

— HNB Life PLC: National IFS Rating upgraded to ‘A+(lka) from ‘A(lka)’; Outlook Stable

— HNB General Insurance Limited (HNBGI): National IFS Rating upgraded to ‘A+(lka) from ‘A(lka)’; Outlook Stable

— People’s Insurance PLC: National IFS Rating upgraded to ‘A+(lka) from ‘A(lka)’; Outlook Stable

— Co-operative Insurance Company PLC (CICPLC): National IFS Rating upgraded to ‘BB+(lka)’ from ‘BB(lka)’; Outlook Stable

— Continental Insurance Lanka Limited (CILL): National IFS Rating affirmed at ‘A(lka)’; Outlook Stable

— Construction Guarantee Fund (CGF): National IFS affirmed at ‘BB(lka)’; Outlook Stable

The insurers’ National Ratings take into consideration their creditworthiness relative to those of other issuers in the country. National scale ratings are a risk ranking of issuers in a particular market designed to help local investors differentiate risk. Sri Lanka’s national scale ratings are denoted by the unique identifier ‘(lka)’. Fitch adds this identifier to reflect the unique nature of the Sri Lankan national scale. National scales are not comparable with Fitch’s international rating scales or with other countries’ national rating scales.

The national scale recalibration reflects changes in the relative creditworthiness of Sri Lankan issuers after Fitch upgraded Sri Lanka’s Long-Term Local-Currency Issuer Default Rating (IDR) to ‘B-‌’ with Stable Outlook from ‘CCC+’ on 22 September 2026. For details, see “Fitch Ratings Recalibrates Sri Lanka’s National Rating Scale”, dated 21 October 2026.

Key Rating Drivers
The National Rating upgrades are driven by the upgrade of Sri Lanka’s Long-Term Local-Currency IDR and the recalibration of the national rating scale and greater room for positive differentiation on the recalibrated national rating scale. The National IFS Rating upgrades of SLIC Life, SLIC General, HNB Life, HNB General, People’s Insurance and CICPLC reflect their relative creditworthiness, as differentiated by their company profiles, capitalization and financial performance.

We believe the sovereign’s credit profile improvement has reduced insurers’ investment and liquidity risks, which are closely linked to those of the sovereign and domestic banks because insurers’ investment portfolios are dominated by local-currency fixed-income government securities, corporate debt and deposits with financial institutions.

SLIC Life

SLIC Life’s rating upgrade reflects its ‘Favorable’ company profile, strong capitalization and strong profitability. SLIC Life and SLIC General are fully owned by the government of Sri Lanka.

Its company profile is supported by its long operating history, extensive franchise and broad distribution network, including a strong agency force. SLIC Life has remained Sri Lanka’s third-largest life insurer for the past three years, with a stable 14% share of life-insurance gross written premiums (GWP).

Capitalization remains a rating strength. SLIC Life maintained a risk-based capital (RBC) ratio above 400% during 2023-2025 and reported a ratio of 478% at end-1H26, exceeding those of Fitch-rated domestic life-insurance peers. SLIC Life’s average return on equity (ROE) of 16% over 2024-2025 has supported internal capital generation.

SLIC General

SLIC General’s rating upgrade reflects its ‘Favorable’ company profile, strong capitalization and strong profitability.

Its company profile is supported by its long operating history, leading franchise and broad distribution network. SLIC General has retained its position as the largest non-life insurer in Sri Lanka since 2024, with a 20% share of non-life GWP in 2025.

Capitalization remains a rating strength. SLIC General maintained an RBC ratio above 250% over the past two years and reported a ratio of 265% at end-1H26 which remains stronger than that of Fitch-rated domestic non-life-insurance peers. SLIC General’s average ROE of 12% and combined ratio of 103% during 2024-2025 compared favorably with Fitch-rated domestic non-life peers, although performance was weighed down by Cyclone Ditwah-related claims in 2025. Fitch expects gradual underwriting improvement through stronger claims management, and pricing discipline.

HNB Life and HNBGI

The upgrades of HNB Life and its wholly owned subsidiary, HNBGI, reflect the group’s ‘Favorable’ company profile, strong group profitability and satisfactory capitalization. Fitch expects HNB Life to provide capital support to HNBGI, if needed, to maintain adequate capital buffers and support business growth.

Their franchises benefit from their association with the parent, Hatton National Bank PLC (National Long-Term Rating: AA-(lka)/Stable), one of Sri Lanka’s largest private commercial banks. HNB Life was the sixth-largest life insurer, with an 8.6% share of life GWP in 2025, while its average GWP growth over 2023-2025 of 30% exceeded the industry average of 19%. HNBGI was the sixth-largest non-life insurer, with a 7.3% share of non-life GWP.

HNB Life’s average ROE was 19% during 2023-2025 while the group’s average ROE of 18% reflects strong profitability. HNBGI’s operating performance has improved, with its annualized ROE rising to 10% in 1H26 from an average of 8% in 2023-2025. Its combined ratio improved to 106% in 1H26, although its three-year average of 109% remained below the industry average.

The group’s capitalization is satisfactory. HNB Life’s RBC ratio remained above 250% in 2023-2025, although below the life-insurance industry average. HNBGI’s RBC ratio declined to 198% by end-1H26, from 219% in 2024.

People’s Insurance

The upgrade reflects People’s Insurance’s improving underwriting performance and strong capitalization.

Its company profile benefits from the People’s brand and its relationship with parent People’s Leasing & Finance PLC (National Long-Term Rating: AA-(lka)/Stable), which supports distribution and contributes materially through the group channel. It is Sri Lanka’s eighth largest non-life insurer in 2025, with a 5.6% share of GWP.

The insurer’s capitalization has been strong compared with rated non-life peers. Its RBC ratio has been above 240% over 2023-2025 and at 241% at end-1H26. Its operating performance has improved, with annualized ROE rising to 12% in 1H26 from 6% in 2025 and exceeding the three-year average of 8%, driven by stronger earnings from tighter underwriting and better investment returns. People’s Insurance’s combined ratio improved to 102% in 1H26, while its three-year average of 113% remained elevated, although below the industry average.

CICPLC

The upgrade reflects CICPLC’s ‘Moderate’ company profile, recovering profitability and satisfactory capitalization.

Fitch has revised CICPLC’s corporate governance assessment to ‘Neutral’ from ‘Less Favorable’, reflecting measures taken over the past two years to address prior weaknesses in its governance structure. CICPLC has an adequate franchise, supported by co-operative-society ownership, with a 3% share of non-life GWP and its position as the tenth-largest insurer in Sri Lanka in 2025.

CICPLC’s operating performance has strengthened from weak historical levels, with annualized ROE rising to 6% in 1H26 from a three-year average of 0.3% and the combined ratio improving to 109% in 1H26, from 115% in 2025. However, profitability and underwriting performance remain weaker than those of higher-rated Fitch-rated domestic non-life peers. Capitalization is satisfactory, with the RBC ratio remaining above 200% in 2023-2025 and standing at 210% at end-1H26.

CILL

CILL’s rating reflects its moderate company profile and satisfactory regulatory capital position, which are offset by its weaker underwriting performance relative to peers.

CILL was the seventh-largest non-life insurer in Sri Lanka in 2025, with a GWP market share of 6.8%. Its business mix is more diversified than that of most domestic non-life insurers, reflecting its larger presence in non-motor business lines. Its regulatory capitalization remained satisfactory, with an RBC ratio of 222% at end-1H26 (end-2025: 230%).

CILL’s underwriting performance weakened in 2025. The combined ratio rose to 119% from 100% in 2024, due to high medical claims and adverse claims development in health. This resulted in a net loss of LKR654 million in 2025 (2024: profit of LKR436 million). Its recent performance has been weak relative to Fitch-rated domestic non-life insurers, with the combined ratio at 113% in 1H26. CILL’s continued losses could weaken its regulatory capitalization.

Ownership of CILL is in the process of being transferred from Melstacorp PLC (National Long-Term Rating: AAA(lka)/Stable) to Janashakthi PLC. Janashakthi proposes to initially acquire an 81% stake in CILL, with the remaining 19% to be transferred in two tranches of 9% and 10% over the subsequent two years. The transaction remains subject to final approval from the Insurance Regulatory Commission of Sri Lanka.

CGF

The affirmation reflects CGF’s ‘Moderate’ company profile and improving operating conditions in Sri Lanka’s construction sector, which are offset by CGF’s historically volatile performance.

CGF is fully state-owned, with the Secretary to the Treasury acting as the trust’s settlor. It serves a niche market by providing guarantees and related services to SME contractors involved in government projects.

A growing foreign-funded infrastructure pipeline supported demand for CGF’s bonds and guarantees, driving a material recovery in core guarantee income in 1H26. CGF’s average ROE was 13% in 2023-2025, although investment income, rather than guarantee operations, remained the main contributor to profitability.

Capitalization was adequate, supported by internally generated surplus and total capital of about LKR2.0 billion at end-2025. Net guarantee risk exposure was modest at 0.6x total equity. However, CGF’s earnings and business volumes remain sensitive to the pace of project implementation and broader conditions in the domestic construction sector.

RATING SENSITIVITIES
Factors that Could, Individually or Collectively, Lead to Negative Rating Action/Downgrade
SLIC Life

– Prolonged weakness in financial performance;

– A deterioration in the RBC ratio to below 300% for a sustained period;

– Rising investment and asset risks, including a downgrade of the ratings of financial institutions or the sovereign, which account for a large share of SLIC Life’s investment portfolio.

SLIC General

– Sustained weakness in financial performance;

– Deterioration in the RBC ratio to below 220% for a sustained period;

– Rising investment and asset risks, including a downgrade of the ratings of financial institutions or the sovereign, which account for a large share of SLIC General’s investment portfolio.

HNB Life and HNBGI

– Deterioration in HNB Life’s RBC ratio to below 240% or a significant deterioration in HNBGI’s capital position for a sustained period;

– Sustained deterioration in financial performance or weaker risk-management practices;

– Rising investment and asset risks, including a downgrade of the ratings of financial institutions or the sovereign.

CICPLC

– Deterioration in the company profile, including a weaker franchise and competitive positioning, or Fitch’s perception that the insurer’s corporate governance practices have deteriorated;

– Sustained deterioration in financial performance, or weaker risk-management practices;

– Rising investment and asset risks, including a downgrade of the ratings of financial institutions or the sovereign.

CILL

– Deterioration in the company profile, including a weaker franchise and competitive positioning, or Fitch’s perception that the insurer’s corporate governance practices have deteriorated;

– Deterioration in the RBC ratio to below 220% for a sustained period;

– Sustained deterioration in financial performance, or weaker risk-management practices;

– Rising investment and asset risks, including downgrades of the ratings on the Sri Lanka sovereign or domestic financial institutions.

People’s Insurance

– Deterioration in the regulatory RBC ratio to below 200% for a sustained period;

– Sustained deterioration in financial performance or weaker risk-management practices;

– Rising investment and asset risks, including a downgrade of the ratings on Sri Lankan financial institutions or the sovereign.

CGF

– Sustained deterioration in financial performance or weaker risk-management practices;

– Deterioration in the company profile, for instance, due to a significant weakening in CGF’s association with the government, or deterioration in its business risk profile due to a decline in the country’s economic conditions that affects the domestic construction sector;

– Rising investment and asset risks, including a downgrade of the ratings of financial institutions or the sovereign.

Factors that Could, Individually or Collectively, Lead to Positive Rating Action/Upgrade
SLIC Life

– Further improvement in the company profile, including a greater operating scale and a stronger market positioning

SLIC General

– Further improvement in the company profile, including a greater operating scale and stronger market position;

– An improvement in the risk-based capital ratio to well above 300% while maintaining the combined ratio at below 95%.

HNB Life and HNBGI

– An improvement in the RBC ratio to well above 320% at HNB Life and 250% at HNBGI, while maintaining the combined ratio below 98% for HNBGI;

– Further improvement in the company profile, for instance, from a stronger business franchise and larger operating scale.

CICPLC

– Further improvement in the company profile, including a stronger business franchise and greater operating scale;

– Maintaining its combined ratio well below 105% for a sustained period, while our assessment of the insurer’s capitalization remains unchanged.

CILL

– Maintaining its combined ratio below 98% for a sustained period, while our assessment of the insurer’s capitalization remains unchanged.

– Sustained improvement in the company profile, including a further expansion in its operating scale and business franchise

People’s Insurance

– An improvement in the RBC ratio to well above 240% and maintaining the combined ratio below 98% consistently for a sustained period;

– Improving the business profile in terms of broader diversification of business lines.

CGF

– Sustained improvement in the company profile in terms of a larger operating scale and successful diversification into profitable and stable business lines.

item.title: Sri Lanka stocks close up 0.66-pct led by banks
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Positive contributors to the ASPI were Commercial Bank, Hatton National Bank, Sri Lanka Telecom, Distilleries Company
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s Colombo Stock Exchange closed up on Thursday, CSE data showed, with the benchmark All Share Price Index moving up 0.66 percent.

The ASPI was up 140.36 points at 21,543.12, while the more liquid S&P SL20 was up 0.85 percent, or 52.07 points, at 6,149.04.

Positive contributors to the ASPI were Commercial Bank of Ceylon (up 0.94 percent at 215.25 rupees), Hatton National Bank (up 0.95 percent at 397 rupees), Sri Lanka Telecom (up 4.94 percent at 93.50 rupees), Distilleries Company of Sri Lanka (up 0.86 percent at 58.60 rupees), and LOLC Holdings (up 2.01 percent at 405.75 rupees).

Hayleys (down 0.75 percent at 232.25 rupees), Bukit Darah (down 2.27 percent at 840 rupees), Richard Pieris and Company (down 1.82 percent at 27 rupees), Malwatte Valley Plantation (down 3.30 percent at 52.80 rupees), and Ambeon Holdings (down 1.44 percent at 34.30 rupees) were top negative contributors.

Market turnover was 1.73 billion rupees. Banks led turnover with 888.06 million rupees. (Colombo/Nov19/2026)
